name: Daron Acemoglu
affiliation: MIT, Institute Professor; 2024 Nobel laureate in economics
view: Acemoglu expects AI to affect about 5% of jobs and does not expect any current occupation to disappear within five to ten years.
quote: I don't expect any occupation that we have today to have been eliminated in five or 10 years' time

source.title: Don't be taken by the hype: MIT economist says AI likely to impact just 5% of jobs (Business Today)

wrong_if: If Amodei and Georgieva are right, entry-level and white-collar displacement arrives this decade and a 5% estimate is too low.
horizon_why: “I don't expect any occupation that we have today to have been eliminated in five or 10 years' time” No occupation gone within a decade reads as slow diffusion.
balance_why: “That's how I arrived at the 5% number.” Small displacement; he also calls current development not pro-human, so not scored higher.

figure.quote: That's how I arrived at the 5% number.

name: Erik Brynjolfsson
view: Brynjolfsson says today's economy sits low on an AI productivity J-curve, where gains dip before climbing, and expects productivity to take off over five years or so.
quote: I’m pretty optimistic about productivity taking off over the next five years or so.

source.title: Erik Brynjolfsson on how AI is rewriting the rules of the economy (Harvard Business School, Managing the Future of Work)

wrong_if: If Acemoglu is right, measured gains stay near 1% of GDP across ten years and no upturn comes on a five-year clock.
horizon_why: “I’m pretty optimistic about productivity taking off over the next five years or so.” Five-year upturn: near term but past the two-year mark.
balance_why: “On average, they were about 14 percent more productive” Gains reported for workers with access, with the bottom 20 percent gaining most.

figure.unit: percent productivity gain per worker (call-centre study)
figure.quote: On average, they were about 14 percent more productive

name: Kristalina Georgieva
view: Georgieva says AI is adding to productivity while countries remain under-prepared for its labor effects, and the IMF assesses 60% of jobs in advanced economies as affected.
quote: It is like a tsunami hitting the labor market, especially in advanced economies, where we assess 60% of jobs to be impacted.

source.title: The IMF's Kristalina Georgieva on the AI 'Tsunami' Hitting the Labor Market (TIME)

wrong_if: If Acemoglu is right, exposure does not turn into job loss at scale and the tsunami framing overstates near-term disruption.
horizon_why: “It is like a tsunami hitting the labor market” Present tense: the effect is under way.
balance_why: “We also see that we remain under-prepared for the impact of AI on the labor market.” Mixed: she also says “It is adding a boost to productivity.” Labor risk weighed slightly heavier.

figure.unit: percent of jobs in advanced economies impacted
figure.quote: where we assess 60% of jobs to be impacted

name: Liz Shuler
view: Shuler launched the AFL-CIO Workers First Initiative on AI with principles that tie AI's economic benefit to workers' rights and shared gains.
quote: We reject the false choice between American competitiveness on the world stage and respecting workers’ rights and dignity.

source.title: The AFL-CIO releases AI Principles for Workers (AFL-CIO Technology Institute)

wrong_if: If Brynjolfsson is right, adoption raises output and pay through firm redesign, and bargaining over AI changes less than the principles assume.
balance_why: Benefit is conditional: “it needs to benefit everyone, not just a select few at the top”. Its principles also aim to “protect working people and the general public from the well-documented negative consequences of unregulated AI”. Both quotes come from that page's principles text.

name: Jason Resnikoff
affiliation: University of Groningen, contemporary history; author of Labor's End
view: Resnikoff compares AI talk to twentieth-century automation discourse and argues that vague use of the term lets people in charge decide what counts as progress.
quote: The rhetoric around it is remarkably vague, and that vagueness is doing a lot of work.

source.title: Jason Resnikoff, US labour historian: “If unions don't ...” (Equal Times)

wrong_if: If Amodei is right about capability, AI has effects of its own beyond management choices and the automation analogy understates it.
balance_why: “lets capital keep control over who gets to benefit from it” Distributional harm is his concern; he calls today's tools “Useful, yes, but not revolutionary”, so no large-displacement score.

name: Fatih Birol
view: Birol's IEA projects data centre electricity use rising from about 415 terawatt-hours in 2024 to 945 by 2030, with America taking the largest share of that increase.
quote: AI is one of the biggest stories in the energy world today

source.title: Data centres to consume more electricity than Japan by 2030 (World Economic Forum)

wrong_if: If smaller, cheaper models win as Nilekani expects, data centre demand grows slower than the 945 TWh path.
horizon_why: “this will more than double to 945 TWh over the next five years” Demand growth is under way and projected to 2030. That sentence is WEF's summary of IEA's report.
balance_why: The page reports demand without a net harm or benefit judgment.

figure.unit: TWh of data centre electricity demand by 2030 (from 415 TWh in 2024)
figure.quote: this will more than double to 945 TWh over the next five years

name: Jeffrey Ding
view: Ding argues that national advantage in AI comes from spreading it across the economy more than from frontier innovation. The United States can win that race, he says, if it keeps talent channels open.
quote: the United States is well positioned to win the artificial intelligence (AI) diffusion race

source.title: Author's Response: Extensions to General-Purpose Technology Diffusion Theory (Asia Policy, NBR)

wrong_if: If Allen is right, access to frontier compute decides the contest and export controls matter more than diffusion capacity.
horizon_why: “whether policymakers can adopt the future-oriented perspective needed for GPT diffusion” Advantage accrues through long-run diffusion; he cites STEM workforce programs as “long-term investments”.
balance_why: The response weighs US-China positioning, not net harm or benefit of AI.

name: Gregory C. Allen
view: Allen argues that US chip export controls have kept Chinese AI firms behind and that sales of Nvidia's H20 chips to China help those firms.
quote: Export controls are one of the absolute critical tools that we have to push back against Chinese policy.

source.title: Export Controls Have Helped Nvidia Stay Ahead of Chinese Rivals, Researcher Says (Communications Daily)

wrong_if: If Ding is right, diffusion and talent decide the outcome and chip controls mainly speed China's own supply chain.
horizon_why: The remarks concern current policy and give no horizon for AI's effects.
balance_why: No net harm or benefit judgment on AI as such; the view is about chip policy.

name: Jack Shanahan
affiliation: Lt Gen, USAF (ret.); first director of the DoD Joint Artificial Intelligence Center
view: Shanahan treats AI as an enabling technology like electricity whose military value depends on diffusion, organizational redesign and new operating concepts over two decades.
quote: What really matters to me is how this technology will diffuse across the military over the next two decades.

source.title: Podcast: Lt Gen Jack Shanahan, USAF (Ret.) on “The Military Uses of Artificial Intelligence” (Lawfire, Duke Law)

wrong_if: If Amodei's timeline holds, human-level systems arrive within years and a two-decade diffusion frame leaves militaries behind.
horizon_why: “how this technology will diffuse across the military over the next two decades. It won’t happen instantly.” Two-decade diffusion.
balance_why: “that’s not a world I’m particularly optimistic about” Said of a fully autonomous future in which machines decide when to initiate conflict; he adds “We’re not there yet”.

figure.unit: years for AI to diffuse across the military

name: Pamela Samuelson
view: Samuelson argues that collective licensing, one blanket payment scheme for training data, is unlikely to work. Each work's contribution to a general model is unclear, and transaction costs would exceed payouts.
quote: Transaction costs would likely swamp payouts

source.title: Generative AI, Copyright and Politics (Pamela Samuelson keynote slides, Silicon Flatirons)

wrong_if: If publishers are right, licensing markets form at scale and transaction costs do not block payment to authors.
balance_why: The slides assess licensing mechanics, not net harm or benefit of AI.

name: Sarah Cardell
affiliation: UK Competition and Markets Authority, Chief Executive
view: Cardell's CMA brought Google's AI Overviews and AI Mode inside its strategic market status designation for search and prioritised remedies for content providers on transparency and attribution.
quote: we decided it was essential to include the use of AI overviews and AI mode

source.title: Promoting competition and protecting consumers to drive growth and improve household prosperity (GOV.UK speech)

wrong_if: If Nilekani is right that models become a commodity, competition among model makers checks market power and designation in advance adds cost.
horizon_why: No horizon; the speech keeps open revisiting Gemini “if the way Gemini was used for search evolved in the future”.
balance_why: The speech's one benefit line (“New technologies are expanding the bounds of human understanding and capability.”) is about technology in general, not AI, so no AI balance is scored.

name: Shannon Vallor
affiliation: University of Edinburgh, Baillie Gifford Chair in the Ethics of Data and AI
view: Vallor argues that AI systems reflect human data without thinking, and that describing them as separate beings misleads people about where agency sits.
quote: A reflection of something is not something, just like the reflection of the mind is not the mind, because this reflection can’t think independently,

source.title: Looking into the AI Mirror with Professor Shannon Vallor (Markkula Center for Applied Ethics, Santa Clara University)

wrong_if: If Amodei is right about systems that outperform humans at nearly everything, the mirror frame understates what the systems do on their own.
balance_why: The article reports her as cautioning against misconceptions rather than weighing net harm or benefit; the framing sentences are the writer's.

name: Carlota Perez
affiliation: UCL Institute for Innovation and Public Purpose; SPRU, University of Sussex
view: Perez treats AI as part of what she counts as the fifth technological revolution and expects a financial crash before its golden age.
quote: I have not seen a golden age happening without a crash,

source.title: Before the golden age of AI must come the crash, history suggests (The Irish Times, from the Financial Times)

wrong_if: If AI revenue keeps pace with capital spending, installation ends without a crash and her cycle does not repeat.
horizon_why: “I have not seen a golden age happening without a crash,” Broad benefits come after a crash still ahead.
balance_why: “This could also be a trigger for gigantic instability,” Near-term financial harm before a later golden age; scored at the midpoint.

name: Nanjira Sambuli
affiliation: Carnegie Endowment for International Peace, nonresident scholar; Ford Global Fellow (Kenya)
view: Sambuli argues that AI skills training in Africa will not create work without job opportunities and infrastructure for using those skills.
quote: Endless skilling will not per se solve for the lack of job opportunities to apply these skills

source.title: Rethinking Skills, AI and the Future of Work in Africa (Veolia Institute)

wrong_if: If Brynjolfsson is right, AI tools raise productivity for small and informal firms directly and skills move ahead of infrastructure.
horizon_why: No horizon for AI's effects; the 2030 date is about workforce growth.
balance_why: The essay conditions outcomes on jobs and infrastructure: “If AI is poised to disrupt what constitute formal sector jobs”.

figure.unit: million new jobs needed in Africa each year
figure.quote: necessitating the creation of 15 million new jobs annually

name: Nandan Nilekani
affiliation: Infosys, co-founder and chairman; architect of Aadhaar
view: Nilekani expects AI models to become a commodity and argues that India's test is making AI accessible to people at scale.

source.title: Why the world should stop obsessing over LLMs (Rest of World)

wrong_if: If Amodei is right, frontier capability compounds and countries without frontier models depend on the few that have them.
horizon_why: “Enterprise AI is rolling out, but relatively slowly” Consumer use is growing now; enterprise diffusion is slow.
balance_why: “population-scale applications using AI, which make a difference to people’s lives” Expects benefit at population scale.

name: Justin Reich
view: Reich says students who use AI to do their work skip the struggle that produces learning, and that free AI offers to schools work as customer acquisition.
quote: when students are using A.I. to do their work, they're not thinking, they're not struggling, and they're not learning.

source.title: Teachers and parents weigh benefits and risks of artificial intelligence in schools (PBS News Hour)

wrong_if: If AI tutoring shows learning gains at scale, his concern holds for unstructured use and not for designed instruction.
horizon_why: “when students are using A.I. to do their work, they're not thinking, they're not struggling, and they're not learning.” The effect is in classrooms now.
balance_why: “giving away ChatGPT is a customer acquisition strategy” Expects learning loss and commercial capture of schools.

name: Eric Topol
affiliation: Scripps Research Translational Institute, founder and director
view: Topol argues that AI reading many kinds of data at once can flag disease risk 10 to 20 years in advance. It draws on new measures such as organ clocks, which track the pace at which each organ ages, and blood biomarkers.
quote: This is a unique moment in medicine.

source.title: Can AI Look at Your Retina and Diagnose Alzheimer's? Eric Topol Hopes So (WIRED)

wrong_if: If Acemoglu is right, clinical adoption stays slow and narrow and earlier detection reaches few patients within a decade.
horizon_why: “This is a unique moment in medicine.” Tools are available now; extending health span is a longer project.
balance_why: “Health span should be extended as close as we can to lifespan, and I think we can do it,” Expects net benefit.

figure.unit: years of advance warning of Alzheimer's risk from the p-tau217 biomarker (up to)
figure.quote: risk of Alzheimer's 10, 15, even 20 years in advance

name: Dario Amodei
view: Amodei argues that AI better than humans at nearly everything could arrive within a few years, and that 2026 stands closer to danger than 2023 did.
quote: we are considerably closer to real danger in 2026 than we were in 2023.
wrong_if: If Acemoglu and Shanahan are right, diffusion takes decades and his timeline mistakes model capability for economic and military effect.
horizon_why: “powerful AI could be as little as 1–2 years away” He adds “it could also be considerably further out.”
balance_why: “we are considerably closer to real danger in 2026 than we were in 2023.” Risk-led essay; he lists mass unemployment among the risks while also aiming for positive outcomes.

figure.unit: year a “country of geniuses” could materialize (approximate)
figure.quote: suppose a literal “country of geniuses” were to materialize somewhere in the world in ~2027
